edges.description: The net defect is the mechanism this model establishes. Nets form on schedule but are histologically abnormal in the adult, with matrix accumulating at the soma and dendrites sparsely covered.

edges.description: Hippocampal long-term potentiation is defective in slices from null animals, and the whole animal shows a severe associative-learning deficit and an abnormal spatial-navigation strategy.

edges.description: The model does not reproduce the motor phenotype this node is proposed to explain. Reflexes and motor capability are reported as normal apart from a rota-rod coordination deficit read as cerebellar, and the opisthotonic posturing and choreoathetosis seen in patients have not been described in any animal model.
edges.limitations: This is the central translational limit of the model. The only published mechanism for the human motor phenotype cannot be tested in the system that carries all the other experimental support for the gene, so the hypothesis remains EMERGING rather than being either confirmed or discarded.

nodes.description: Perineuronal nets still appear on the normal developmental schedule in tenascin-R-deficient animals, but their architecture is wrong: matrix accumulates on the soma while dendritic coverage is sparse, and the nets around parvalbumin-expressing GABAergic interneurons are markedly underdeveloped. The claim curated here is a structural and distributional defect in the net, not a failure of the net to form at all.

nodes.description: Absence or functional loss of tenascin-R from the extracellular matrix of the central nervous system. The deficit is confined to the central nervous system because tenascin-R is expressed nowhere else, and it is most consequential after birth, when the protein's expression peaks and perineuronal nets are being built. Oligodendrocytes and their precursors are the principal source.
